## QUESTION 1

<!-- Make sure at least one of your charts includes reference marks!! -->

__Make a new column that represents the total number of babies with your name for only those states in which you have lived. (If you have only ever lived in one state, pick at least one other state so you get practice summing across columns). Make a graph displaying that total for your name over time.__

My name is Davi, which translated to David in English. I have lived in Idaho and my family in Tennesee, so I picked those two states for my analysis. I learned that the most popular time for my name was the 1950s.

_AI use reflection_
**Link** to the original chat:
**The Process** How exactly did you use the tool?
**The Impact**  How did using AI impact your learning?

```{python}
# Q1

davi_sum_TN_ID = df.filter(pl.col("name") == "David").select(
    ["name","year", "ID", "TN"]
).with_columns(
    (pl.col("ID") + pl.col("TN")).alias("total_per_state")
)
( 
    ggplot(davi_sum_TN_ID, aes(x="year", y="total_per_state")) +
    geom_line(color="blue") +
    geom_vline(xintercept=1950, color="red", linetype="dashed") +
    labs(title="Total Babies Named David in Idaho and Tennessee", 
         x="Year", 
         y="Total Babies Named David") + theme_minimal() )
```


## QUESTION 2

1. __Let's look at a name that is special for members of the church: Brigham. For each year, calculate what proportion of babies named Brigham were born in Idaho and Utah? Make a graph displaying the proportion over time.__  

From 1971 to 1987, the proportion of babies named Brigham in Idaho and Utah was 100%. After 1987, there were more babies named brigham outside of Idaho and Utah for 5 years. After 1992, the proportion of babies named Brigham in Idaho and Utah was 100% again, and it vaired ever since.

_AI use reflection_
**Link** to the original chat:
**The Process** How exactly did you use the tool?
**The Impact**  How did using AI impact your learning?

```{python}
# Q2
brigham = df.filter(pl.col("name") == "Brigham").select(
    ["name","year", "ID", "UT", "Total"]
).with_columns(
    ((pl.col("ID") + pl.col("UT")) / pl.col("Total")).alias("proportion_per_state"))
( 
    ggplot(brigham, aes(x="year", y="proportion_per_state")) +
    geom_line(color="blue") +
    labs(title="Proportion of Babies Named Brigham in Idaho and Utah", 
         x="Year", 
         y="Proportion") + theme_minimal() )

```

## QUESTION 3

1. __Consider doing some data validation. For the name David, calculate a sum of all 50 states and District of Columbia for each year. Now compare that total to the value in the 'Total' column. In which years, if any, do they not agree?__

They agree in all.

_AI use reflection_
**Link** to the original chat:
**The Process** How exactly did you use the tool?
**The Impact**  How did using AI impact your learning?

```{python}
# Q3
state_cols = [col for col in df.columns if col not in ["name", "year", "Total"]]

david_validation = (
    df.filter(pl.col("name") == "David")
    .with_columns(pl.sum_horizontal(state_cols).alias("calculated_total"))
    .filter(pl.col("calculated_total") != pl.col("Total")))
david_validation

```
